$comment: Behavioural conformance for the pure decision logic, executed by BOTH runtimes, and
the good/bad references every gate must prove before a run starts.
Why this file exists: tests/test_parity.py proves a marker STRING exists in each
build. That catches a feature nobody ported; it cannot catch a feature ported
WRONGLY, and it once passed a row whose JS marker was a comment describing the
mechanism. Every drift this repo has recorded was in logic of exactly this shape: a
pure function over plain data. So both runtimes are asked the same questions here and
must return the same answers.
`instruments` says what each function IS. A `gate` accepts or rejects, so it carries
both a `good` reference it must accept and a `bad` one it must catch, and the
structural rule below is enforced on it. A `transform` maps input to output with no
verdict, so good/bad does not apply and only the answers are checked.
THE STRUCTURAL RULE: every gate must have at least one `good` case and at least one
`bad` case, and in each runtime the bad references must produce at least one answer
no good reference produces. A gate whose bad references all answer the same as its
good ones has not been shown to reject anything, and a check that cannot fail is
indistinguishable from no check. This is the rule the parity markers failed for
years, and the rule catchRate failed by counting a partial as a catch.
It runs at preflight, before any API call, not only in CI: a deployed copy with a
broken gate refuses to start rather than producing a report nobody can check.
A case may carry `out_by_runtime` instead of `out` when the two builds legitimately
answer differently because the PLATFORM differs - URL parsing is the real instance.
That is not an escape hatch for drift: it pins both answers, so either one moving is
a failure, and `why` must say what makes the difference correct.
`python_cases` holds gates the JS build genuinely does not have, each with the reason,
the same way tests/test_parity.py keeps PYTHON_ONLY honest.

webtext.why: a cap TRUNCATES. The JS helper took one parameter for months while seven call sites passed a length, so JavaScript discarded it in silence and shipped untruncated model text into prompts the Python twin bounded
a string under the cap is returned whole, with no ellipsis
null becomes an empty string, not the text 'null' - String(null) in JS gives 'null' and would have put that word in a prompt
tabs and newlines collapse, so a model cannot forge prompt structure with whitespace

tier_of.why: www. is stripped before the host rule runs
the ORIGINAL drift: T4 discovery-only in Python, T3 citable in JS, while the marker row for tierOf passed the whole time
excluded-grade content farm - JS had no T5 host list at all
a resolver is not a publisher: provenance is unverified until it is followed
an unclassified host defaults to the practitioner tier, never to excluded
userinfo before @ is NOT the host - grading this T2 would let any URL borrow a trusted domain's tier

as_list.why: a double-encoded array is recovered, not discarded - it arrived as a JSON string holding the items
and so is a tag-wrapped one
a real array passes through untouched
a missing field is an empty list, never a crash

host_ambiguous.why: an ordinary URL is not ambiguous
and neither is ordinary userinfo: both parsers read nature.com

an IPv6 literal IS ambiguous in both builds - the host regex stops at the first colon and reads '[' while the standard parser reads '[::1]'. Found by probing THIS gate for a reference it actually catches, which is the point of the rule

Nudges remain broadly effective: bias-corrected effect sizes are attenuated but still meaningfully positive
same_hypothesis.why: an 'H1:' relabelling still matches the hypothesis it adjudicates

in: Minimum wage increases reduce employment, and the reduction persists for at least a decade after passage
same_hypothesis.why: a post-hoc SUPERSET is not pre-registered: it contains the registered text and all its content words, which is why min()-denominator overlap scored it 1.0
two OPPOSITE terse hypotheses are not the same one - the character fallback both builds used scored this pair 1.000 and 0.941

in: Nudges remain broadly effective across behavioural domains
same_hypothesis.why: an invented hypothesis does not match, or the stamp means nothing
an empty side never matches, so a missing hypothesis is never called pre-registered

in: H1: Minimum wage rises modestly lower teen employment over the first two years
Minimum wage increases reduce teen employment modestly in the first two years
hyp_unrelated.why: a genuine rewording naming the right number is still believed: this overrules on SUBJECT, never on wording

in: The minimum wage increase caused a decade-long employment decline across all age groups
Minimum wage increases reduce teen employment modestly in the first two years
hyp_unrelated.why: a verdict whose text adjudicates something never registered is caught whatever number it declares - hypothesisNumber was authoritative with nothing examined

shape_problems.why: an EMPTY string passes: an auditor that legitimately found no quote must be able to say so
an integral float is accepted: JSON has no int/float distinction, so 3.0 and 3 are the same value
a declared string rejects a number - `required` only ever meant key-present, which hollowed out the locatedQuote fix in both builds
ADR-0001: the seam retries rather than coerces, and int('5') was the one leaf violating it
a fractional float is data loss - truncating it landed a coverage row in the wrong sub-question bucket
a bool is not an integer, even though Python says isinstance(True, int)
and the string 'true' is not a boolean
a missing required key is still a problem - this is what `required` always did mean

quote_span.why_python_only: Locating a quote needs the exact page text the extractor was shown, and in the JS build that text never reaches the orchestrator - its extract subagent calls the runtime's WebFetch itself and returns only the claim.

in: The trial found that profits rose 3 percent in the treated arm, a result the authors attribute to scheduling effects rather than headcount, and the effect persisted at 12 months.
profits rose 3 percent in the treated arm
cases.why: a quote that is on the page is found

in: The trial found that profits rose 3 percent in the treated arm, a result the authors attribute to scheduling effects rather than headcount, and the effect persisted at 12 months.

is_prose.why_python_only: The Python build parses PDF bytes itself, so it can measure whether the result is readable prose. The JS build never sees bytes.

in: The study found that participants who used standing desks reported less discomfort over the twelve week period, although the authors note that the effect was concentrated among those who had previously reported back pain, and that the sample was drawn from a single office in one city, which limits how far the result can reasonably be generalised to other workplaces.
cases.why: real English prose passes both signals

in: Cette etude montre que les participants ayant utilise des bureaux debout ont signale moins de gene pendant la periode de douze semaines, bien que les auteurs notent que cet effet etait concentre parmi ceux qui avaient deja signale des douleurs dorsales, et que echantillon provenait un seul bureau dans une seule ville, ce qui limite la portee du resultat pour autres lieux de travail.
cases.why: and so does a NON-ENGLISH paper - high letter ratio, zero English stopwords. This is the good reference the 'BOTH signals must fail' rule exists to protect, and the first bad reference written for this gate was a navigation wordlist, which is readable text and correctly passed. Writing the reference is what revealed that this gate detects binary wearing a text costume, not boilerplate

a PDF with a broken ToUnicode map is caught: 43% letters, 0.0 stopwords per 1000 chars, past the 40-word floor so it is the RATIO rule doing the work. digamoo.free.fr/neumark1994.pdf sailed through the old guard and the model returned four fluent, entirely invented quotes from it
